description: The Lectio Edition of Homer's Iliad: a prose Iliad in plain current English, with its choices, its opening, and the record of its review.
what: Homer's poem of a few weeks in the tenth year of the war at Troy. It is about what a man does with anger, with grief, and with the certainty that he will die. The Greeks sang it for centuries before anyone wrote it down.
why_title: Homer is fast. The old English versions are slow.
why: The two public-domain Iliads most people find are Pope's couplets of 1715 and Butler's prose of 1898. Pope is a great English poem and not much like Homer. Butler is plain, but he gives the gods their Roman names and writes "car" for chariot.
A reader who starts either one tends to stop in Book II. The story is not the obstacle. The English is.

The Lectio Edition is a prose Iliad in current English, all twenty-four books. It keeps the repeated epithets, because the repetition is how the poem is built. It restores the Greek names. Pope and Butler stay in the app beside it.
choices_lede: These are the rules the review settled for the whole poem.
choices: The first word, *menis*, is "rage". The hot human anger Achilles later curses, *cholos*, is "anger". The two are kept apart, as Homer keeps them.
The army is mostly "the Greeks". Homer's three names for it, Achaeans, Argives and Danaans, mean the same coalition and were chosen to fit the meter.
Gods and heroes have their Greek names: Zeus, Hera, Athena, Odysseus.
Fixed epithets are kept each time they recur: swift-footed Achilles, Hector breaker of horses.
A patronymic that names a remote ancestor is given as descent. Achilles is "grandson of Aeacus", not his son.
No Biblical or Christian idiom in a pagan poem, and no modern slang. The draft had "the spirit may be willing", "a time to mourn" and "blowhard". All were replaced with what the Greek says.
"Car" became "chariot" in 53 places, and leftover archaisms such as "chine" and "a whit" were replaced.

divergences.why: The poem's first word. Homer uses it almost only for the anger of gods. "Rage" is the current word nearest to its size.
Three names for one army. Keeping all three puzzles a new reader and tells him nothing. The introduction records the variety.

divergences.older: "Like leaves on trees the race of man is found" (Pope)
divergences.lectio: The generations of men are like the leaves of the trees.
divergences.why: The most quoted lines in the book. Butler has the forest bud with "fresh vines", which is a slip. The Greek is leaves falling and the same tree leafing again.

divergences.older: "it can neither be bought nor harried back again" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: a man's life cannot be raided back
divergences.why: Achilles uses of his life the same words he has just used of cattle and tripods. Everything Agamemnon offers can be replaced. A life cannot. The edition keeps the raiding words.
When Achilles curses the passion that rose in him against Agamemnon, Homer does not use the word of line one. The edition reserves "rage" for *menis* so the reader can feel the difference.

divergences.older: "Therefore, my friend, you too shall die" (Butler)
divergences.why: Achilles calls the boy he is about to kill *philos*, one of his own. He is not being kind. He is counting Lycaon among the doomed, himself included. The address is kept bare.

divergences.older: "And peaceful slept the mighty Hector's shade" (Pope, who rewrites the ending)
divergences.lectio: Such was the funeral of Hector, breaker of horses.
divergences.why: The poem ends on Hector, on a burial, and on an epithet. The edition ends where Homer ends.

checked: Butler (1898) and Pope (1715). The Greek is not in the bundle, so the Greek readings came from the reviewing model's own knowledge of the text.
open: The editor's own read of all twenty-four books.

Book I: Achilles' retelling of the quarrel to Thetis is 28 lines of speech in Homer. The edition still gives it as a short narrated list. It has to be restored as speech, and that is new writing the editor should read.
Three segments are set aside, in Books V, X and XXIII. The editor has to decide whether to retire them for good or replace them with Homer's own closing lines.
The note that stood at the end of Book XXIII should move to the margin notes.
